A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same conjugate moment measure framework. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including proofs, experimental appendices, figures and tables, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original experiments on univariate Gaussian mixtures, five synthetic 2D distributions and MNIST generation.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B–E report original sample-based and energy-based experiments, quantitative ICNN comparisons, Cartoon generation and image reconstruction.

M1.justification: The original fixed-point learner is retained as CMFGen. v2 adds CMFMA, which learns from an unnormalized density through a Monge–Ampère regression objective involving the Hessian determinant (Section 4.3). It also replaces fixed LMC step sizes with a Hessian-adaptive rule and introduces learned-density optimization for inpainting.

E1.justification: The original Gaussian mixtures, five synthetic 2D distributions and MNIST remain. v2 adds the Cartoon dataset, three energy-defined 2D target distributions, learning with energy-function access, and reconstruction of half-masked MNIST and Cartoon images. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Gaussian-to-data generative ICNN baselines for the retained 2D datasets and MNIST, as well as Cartoon (Figures 13, 5 and 15). Amos (2023) supplied a solver in v1 but was not evaluated there as this generative comparator. The original standard moment-measure comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 revise reported training budgets: 2D gradient steps increase from 700,000 to 1,000,000, MNIST steps decrease from 100,000 to 50,000, and generation-time LMC steps increase from 6,000 to 10,000. Diag-Checkerboard batches change from 4,096 to 1,024. v2 also introduces architecture-matched baseline comparisons, Sinkhorn evaluation with 2,048-sample batches, and half-image masking protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds brief qualitative sensitivity and failure analyses: reducing training LMC steps to 50 degrades performance, and ELU activations cause discontinuities in learned 1D CMFMA potentials, motivating Softplus. These are limited supplementary observations rather than a substantial ablation or robustness study.

E5.justification: v1 provides no seed-based variability assessment. v2 introduces evaluations across 100 random seeds and boxplots of Sinkhorn divergences for all five 2D datasets (Appendix D.1, Figure 13). This establishes a new variability-reporting practice. The seeds vary generated and reference samples; 100 independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds quantitative Sinkhorn comparisons, CMFMA energy-fitting and pushforward results, Cartoon generation, and MNIST/Cartoon reconstruction outcomes. Figure 13 shows broadly overlapping ICNN and CMFGen distributions with modest differences. The original 1D findings remain, including v1 Figure 5 as v2 Figure 8. Revised settings prevent interpreting refreshed generation examples as controlled before-and-after performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds the Monge–Ampère density and energy characterizations in equations (8)–(9), providing the mathematical basis for energy-based learning, and an additional variational proof of Proposition 1. It corrects the 1D transport formula from B to its gradient and removes the earlier entropy–OT variational formulation. The central existence theorem and Schauder proof are retained; v1 Theorem 2 becomes Appendix A's Lemma 1.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion expand the methodological contribution from learning a conjugate potential using samples to learning it using either samples or an unnormalized target density. The central factorization claim and claimed first ICNN generation of MNIST remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: The interpretation that conjugate Gibbs factors better match target distributions remains. v2 adds explanations of ELU/Hessian difficulties, the LMC efficiency–quality tradeoff, and why ordinary moment-potential regression is harder. It removes v1's concluding qualification that ICNN training difficulties currently hinder performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds code listings for the previously described 1D algorithms (Appendix B.3), explicit benchmark energy formulas, quadratic-input architecture details, and CMFMA hyperparameter tables, including Softplus with beta 10. It documents Cartoon preprocessing with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.2. Reported hardware changes from V100 or A100-40GB to V100-32GB.

R1.justification: The main moment-measure and optimal-transport positioning remains. v2 adds Dalalyan (2016), Ramdas et al. (2017), Rezende and Mohamed (2015), and Royer et al. (2018), supporting sampling, evaluation, the normalizing-flow analogy and Cartoon data. It also explicitly positions its ordinary moment-measure solver as addressing a previously unavailable method.

P1.justification: Existing material is substantially reorganized: Background is condensed, the main proof sketch moves to Appendix A, the univariate transport recipe moves from experiments into methods, and the fixed-point method is named CMFGen. The methods and experimental narratives are rewritten, and the appendix is reorganized into separate theory, sample-based, energy-based, evaluation and implementation sections.

P2.justification: The 2D display changes from two rows with overlaid targets and potentials to three separate rows. MNIST receives a baseline-comparison panel, while Cartoon uses the earlier schematic format. New energy plots, Sinkhorn boxplots and reconstruction grids substantially expand the visual evidence. Hyperparameter tables separate shared solver settings and add CMFMA configurations; the original 1D convergence display is retained.

improvement.justification: v1's practical generative claims relied mainly on qualitative demonstrations. v2 materially strengthens their assessment through architecture-matched ICNN comparisons and repeated sample-level quantitative evaluations (Appendix D.1), while adding a tested energy-based method and substantial reproducibility details. Image evaluation remains qualitative, the earlier general training caveat is removed, and Section 4.3 contains a log-determinant sign inconsistency with equation (9). These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support, methodological utility and reproducibility.
